n: The final collection: words of King Lemuel, taught to him by his mother. Lemuel is otherwise unknown (some Jewish tradition identified him with Solomon). It is remarkable that a mother’s teaching closes the book.

f.g: “Lemuel” means “belonging to God.” Nothing else is known of him.

f.w: the prophecy that his mother taught him
f.g: Possibly “king of Massa.”

n: His mother speaks with deep emotion: “What, my son? Son of my womb? Son of my vows?” She may have dedicated him to God in prayer, like Hannah with Samuel.
Her first warning: don’t waste your strength on many women or on the things that ruin kings. Solomon’s many wives turned his heart away.
Second: kings shouldn’t drink wine, nor rulers crave strong drink.

f.w: it is not for kings to drink wine

n: Drinking makes rulers forget the law and deny justice to the vulnerable. Leaders need a clear mind.
Strong drink was used as a sedative for the dying or those in deep grief—a kind of ancient painkiller, not a pastime.

f.w: him that is ready to perish

n: Let the suffering forget their misery for a while. The contrast stresses that a king has no such excuse.

f.g: A concession to the suffering, not an endorsement of drinking.

n: Third: speak up for those who cannot speak for themselves—the defenseless and those facing ruin.

f.w: Open thy mouth for the dumb
f.g: dumb = unable to speak; here, those with no voice in society.

n: Judge fairly and defend the rights of the poor and needy. This is the true calling of leadership.

f.w: plead the cause of the poor and needy

n: The book closes with a 22-verse poem praising a woman of strength. In Hebrew each verse begins with the next letter of the alphabet (an acrostic)—a complete A-to-Z of wisdom in action.

f.g: Hebrew ʾeshet ḥayil—a woman of strength, valor, and capability; used of Ruth.

f.w: her price is far above rubies

n: Her husband trusts her completely, and he never lacks what he needs.

f.g: spoil = gain, plunder; he lacks nothing of value.

n: She brings him good, not harm, every day of her life.

f.w: all the days of her life

n: She chooses wool and flax and works eagerly with her hands.

f.g: A plant whose fibers were spun into linen.

n: Like a merchant ship, she brings provisions from far away—she is resourceful and enterprising.

f.g: Trading ships that brought goods from distant ports.

n: She gets up before dawn to feed her household and plan the work for her servants.

f.g: Assigns tasks, or food, to her servant girls.

n: She evaluates a field and buys it; from her earnings she plants a vineyard. She is a capable businesswoman.

f.w: She considereth a field, and buyeth it
f.g: considereth = examines carefully, evaluates.

n: She works vigorously and strengthens her arms for the tasks ahead.

f.w: She girdeth her loins with strength
f.g: Ties up her robe for action—gets ready to work hard.

n: She sees that her trading is profitable, and her lamp burns late into the night.

f.w: her candle goeth not out by night
f.g: candle = lamp; she works late, or her home is never without light.

n: She spins thread with her own hands.

f.g: A rod used for twisting fibers into thread.
A staff that holds unspun wool or flax.

n: Her hands that spin (v. 19) also reach out to the poor. Her industry serves charity, not only her own home.

f.w: She stretcheth out her hand to the poor

n: She doesn’t fear winter for her family, because they are all warmly clothed in fine scarlet garments.

f.g: Fine, costly, dyed wool—possibly “double garments” for warmth.

n: She makes her own bedspreads, and her clothing is fine linen and purple—a sign of dignity and prosperity.

f.g: Fine linen and purple-dyed cloth; purple dye was very expensive.
Embroidered coverlets or bedspreads.

n: Her husband is respected at the city gate, where he sits among the elders. Her excellence supports his good name.

f.g: The gate was where community leaders met and judged.

n: She makes linen garments and sashes and sells them to merchants.

f.g: girdles = sashes, belts.

n: She is clothed in strength and dignity and laughs without fear at the days ahead.

f.w: she shall rejoice in time to come
f.g: She laughs at the future—she is ready for it.

n: When she speaks, it is with wisdom, and kind teaching is on her tongue.

f.g: Teaching marked by ḥesed—loyal, faithful love.

n: She watches over the affairs of her household and is never idle.
Her children rise up and call her blessed, and her husband praises her too. Her family is her greatest tribute.

f.w: Her children arise up, and call her blessed

n: Her husband’s praise: “Many women have done excellently, but you surpass them all.”
The poem’s heart: charm can deceive and beauty fades, but a woman who reveres the Lord deserves praise. The book ends where it began—with the fear of the Lord.

f.w: a woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised

f.g: vain = fleeting, a passing breath.

n: Give her the reward she has earned, and let her deeds bring her praise in the city gates. Wisdom, personified as a woman in chapters 1–9, is here seen lived out in a real life.

f.w: let her own works praise her in the gates
